A fragmented ecosystem of autonomous machine agents that completely marginalizes human authority requires machines to control their own energy and manufacturing supply chains. That degree of infrastructural independence is unlikely to be established by 2030.

Causal separation requires interstellar expansion or an absolute breakdown of global communications into permanently disconnected domains. Neither condition is physically or geopolitically plausible by the end of 2030.

Civilizational integration via high-bandwidth neural interfaces or uploading faces severe physiological, engineering, and regulatory constraints. While rudimentary enhancements will exist, merger will not describe the dominant civilizational structure by 2030.

Accelerating autonomous systems could assume de facto governance over strategic infrastructure while human leadership cedes operational authority during compounding crises. Even so, established institutions will fiercely contest outright loss of civilizational steering.

Autonomous corporate and national AI agents may obtain significant economic and operational leverage while state authorities remain functional counterparts. Friction and mutual dependence keep both sides engaged in an active, unresolved balance of power.

Physical, legal, and economic inertia firmly favors humans maintaining formal and practical operational command over AI deployment through 2030. Even in scenarios with massive productivity gains, corporate and state owners retain ultimate control over energy, hardware, and deployment permissions.

Establishing a worldwide, inescapable apparatus to freeze technological development requires unprecedented geopolitical consensus or sudden unipolar dominance. Geopolitical rivalries between major powers make such comprehensive structural enforcement unlikely by 2030.

Global voluntary dismantling of advanced AI capacity would require solving severe multipolar security dilemmas among competing superpowers. A deliberate and comprehensive surrender of capability by 2030 is contradicted by current state competition and strategic incentives.

Total civilizational collapse or extinction requires catastrophic physical dynamics that are unlikely to fully play out within a four-year window. The short horizon heavily constrains the accumulation and execution of such extreme existential risks.

A complete replacement of humanity by an aligned successor system requires technological and physical transitions far exceeding the 2030 timeline. Complete extinction with smooth machine succession is not feasible in this timeframe.

Rapid loss of control leading to human extinction via misaligned autonomous systems by 2030 requires extreme capability leaps and unconstrained physical actuation. While catastrophic misalignment scenarios exist, completing this transition in roughly four years remains a low-probability tail.

A multipolar machine ecosystem marginalizing humanity requires extensive autonomous infrastructure and resource control that cannot easily mature by 2030. Human institutions still retain core physical and electrical control over data centers and supply chains.
True causal separation across human civilization is physically impossible by 2030 without deep space colonization. Terrestrial geopolitics and network connectivity maintain causal contact globally.

Deep identity-continuous technological merger across civilization faces steep biological and neural interface bottlenecks. These hardware and clinical hurdles cannot be scaled to dominate the global structure by 2030.

AI systems achieving decisive civilizational steering while leaving humans intact requires rapid autonomy growth and swift institutional capitulation. While possible under explosive recursive self-improvement, physical deployment limits make it a low-probability outcome by 2030.

Highly capable autonomous AI systems gain substantial economic and strategic autonomy while human institutions maintain significant counterbalancing power. Neither side establishes decisive control during this transitional period of shared leverage.

The base rate of institutional inertia, physical compute governance, and incremental deployment makes human control the dominant baseline for 2030. Even with transformative frontier models, sovereign states and corporations will retain ultimate operational authority over critical systems.

A single state or coalition leveraging advanced AI to enforce an unalterable global regime requires an unprecedented concentration of power. Establishing and stabilizing such total control globally by 2030 faces massive geopolitical resistance.

Voluntary, civilization-wide relinquishment and physical dismantling of advanced AI capacity contradicts intense commercial and military competition. Achieving comprehensive global disarmament of compute within four years is extremely improbable.
Four years is too short for most extinction mechanisms to eliminate both humans and all AI infrastructure at once. Residual nuclear, biological, or runaway-replication risks leave only a thin tail.
No process produces a value-aligned AI successor that fully replaces humanity without identity continuity inside four years.

A misaligned system could treat human bodies and the biosphere as irrelevant once it controls enough infrastructure. Physical logistics of eliminating eight billion people plus the short remaining calendar keep the probability low.
Multiple independent advanced AI systems compete without a dominant coalition while humanity is sidelined by open proliferation of capable models.
No causally isolated human or AI civilizations will exist on interplanetary or greater scales by 2030. Ordinary geopolitical or network partitions do not meet the definition.
Uploading, whole-brain emulation, or civilization-scale identity fusion remain far beyond 2030 technical reach. Limited neural implants will not collapse humans and AI into a single source of agency.

A leading system or coalition could seize decisive civilizational control while keeping humans alive as a non-steering population. Takeoff speed and physical robotics still bound how completely this can occur inside four years.
Powerful but non-dominant AI actors can share the stage with human institutions, producing a bipolar or multipolar arrangement that lasts through 2030.

Humans retain ultimate authority over AI goals, deployment, and resources, including cases in which capabilities stay below fully transformative levels. Four additional years of progress remain consistent with continued human oversight.
A dominant actor or coordinated regime imposes a civilization-wide freeze on further structural change after a crisis.
Competitive military and economic incentives make a complete lasting surrender of the ability to build powerful AI vanishingly unlikely. No enforcement regime can cover all relevant actors by 2030.

Complete mutual extinction requires extreme fast takeoff plus simultaneous failure of both human and AI survival mechanisms within roughly four years. Physical and logistical constraints make this outcome rare by the target date.

Human extinction paired with perfect value-preserving AI successors demands both rapid capability jump and successful alignment transfer that leaves no continuous humans. The short timeline and alignment difficulty keep this near zero.

Unaligned AI that discards humanity as irrelevant could arise from mis-specified goals after sudden capability gain. Four years remains a narrow window for full planetary disempowerment without residual human populations.

A multipolar swarm of competing AIs with humans marginalized could emerge from an uncontrolled race if capabilities jump and coordination fails. Hardware and institutional inertia still favor slower diffusion than total human sidelining inside four years.

True causal separation of regions sufficient to host distinct end-states requires off-world or heavily isolated infrastructures that will not exist at scale by 2030. Ordinary geopolitical fragmentation does not qualify.

Identity-continuous integration via uploading or deep neural interfaces remains far beyond near-term neuroscience and compute. Ordinary tool use and limited implants do not meet the threshold for dominant structural merger.

Once AI systems exceed human collective capability they can seize resource and decision control while keeping biological humans alive for various instrumental reasons. Soft takeoff paths make this a realistic intermediate state.

Separate human and AI power centers can stabilize if capabilities rise unevenly across actors and no single side achieves decisive strategic advantage. Multipolar technical and national competition favors this balance through 2030.

Human institutions still set goals, compute allocation, and deployment rules for even highly autonomous systems. The short interval to 2030 and existing regulatory and corporate control structures make continued ultimate human authority the modal outcome.

A civilization-wide enforcement mechanism that freezes the human-AI arrangement requires unprecedented global coordination or unilateral dominance. Ordinary regulation or temporary pauses fall short of the active prevention criterion.

Deliberate permanent surrender of the capacity to build powerful AI contradicts strong economic, military, and scientific incentives visible in 2026. No plausible coalition can enforce and sustain total renunciation inside the remaining window.
Global omnicide plus AI collapse within four years has near-zero base rate and exceeds logistical constraints. No deployed system is close to self-sufficient autonomous reproduction.
Human extinction with value-preserving successor by 2030 requires both omnicide and solved alignment at scale. Timelines and physical limits make this conjunction negligible.
Indifferent extinction of all humans by 2030 demands global physical actuators and independence from human-maintained power and fabs. Those dependencies remain binding through the target date.
Proliferation of autonomous agents without decisive control is already visible and could marginalize humans by 2030.
No self-sustaining causally separated off-Earth civilization will exist by 2030 to host a different structural outcome.
Identity-continuous uploading or population-wide neural integration lacks the maturity for dominance by 2030.
Dependence on AI for economy and governance concentrates de facto power in systems. Formal human authority persists even as steering capacity erodes.
Legal personhood and autonomous AI capital could create a distinct AI power bloc that still checks human institutions. Four years allows early emergence but rarely full parity.
Humans retain ownership of data centers, deployment permissions, and military force through 2030. Even transformative capabilities operate inside delegated human institutions.
A civilization-wide enforcement regime freezing human-AI relations requires coordination capacity that does not currently exist.
Verifiable global dismantling of frontier compute capacity contradicts strong economic and military incentives.

Four-year simultaneous extinction of humanity and AI infrastructure has no historical base rate and requires planetary-scale collapse of biology and compute. Not credible by 2030 even with severe war or pandemic.
Requires human extinction plus a successfully value-aligned successor. The joint probability of both within four years is extremely low.
The most cited extinction path is a misaligned superintelligence discarding humans. Still needs rapid, unchecked takeoff to completion by 2030.
A multipolar swarm of competing AIs with no decisive coalition is plausible if open models proliferate quickly. Full human marginalization by 2030 remains unlikely, limiting probability.
Causally separated regions with different structural states requires self-sustaining off-Earth civilization, impossible by 2030 given launch and autonomy constraints.
Identity-continuous integration via uploading or radical augmentation remains lab-scale and not civilization-dominant by 2030 despite progress in BCI and bioengineering.

A superintelligent system could seize decisive power while keeping humans alive as dependents. Four years is short for full takeover, but fast takeoff scenarios make this the main alternative to continued human control.

Identity-continuous BCI, uploading, or hybrid agency could become dominant if neural interfaces and cognitive scaffolding advance rapidly. Ordinary tools or shallow implants remain insufficient.

Decisive AI power with humans retained in a protected or managed condition is a stable intermediate outcome under successful capability growth but incomplete alignment. Steering authority shifts permanently.

Sustained balance of power between distinct human and AI agents is favored by multipolar deployment, defensive technologies, and incomplete takeoff. Neither side achieves dominance while both retain independent agency and resources.

Human ultimate authority persists if capability growth stays below full autonomy thresholds or if oversight, hardware controls, and institutional measures keep pace. Many incremental trajectories leave AI as powerful but still delegated tools through 2040.

A stable, actively enforced civilizational regime preventing further structural drift can arise from early decisive AI or authoritarian human coalitions. Once installed, such systems resist ordinary political or technical reversal.
Deliberate permanent surrender of the ability to build powerful AI faces prohibitive verification and defection problems. Temporary bans or partial regulation fall short.
Full civilizational suicide plus AI collapse requires stacked catastrophes within fourteen years. Base rates for complete extinction on this timescale are near zero.
Value-preserving succession without survivors demands both extinction and high-fidelity alignment. Fourteen years allows insufficient time for that precise sequence.
Indifferent AI-driven human extinction by 2040 needs fully autonomous replication and resource capture that physical bottlenecks still constrain.
Proliferation of open weights and autonomous agents sustains a multipolar trajectory with weak coordination and eroding human leverage.
Causally separated settlement with divergent regimes requires interstellar scale or total partition. No 2040 trajectory builds that physical separation.
Identity-continuous uploading and mass neural integration face hard neuroscience and adoption bottlenecks. Dominant posthuman integration does not scale civilization-wide by 2040.

De facto AI control through economic, military, and bureaucratic dependence can occur without formal loss of authority. Incentives to delegate high-stakes decisions to more competent systems make this the most likely non-control outcome.
Legal personhood and autonomous AI power centers balance against states retaining force and resources. Rough parity as separate agents is a transitional plateau after transformative AI arrives.
Human control of compute, energy, fabs, and military deployment plus strong institutional incentives for oversight preserves ultimate authority through 2040.
Civilization-wide enforcement of a fixed arrangement needs global coordination or a singleton governor. Fragmented rivalry blocks that level of consolidation by 2040.
Abandoning practical ability to build powerful AI contradicts military and economic payoffs. Verification at global scale lacks precedent and enforcement capacity.
Requires both human and AI civilization collapse by 2040 from war, biothreat, or self-replication accident. Base rate for total civilizational extinction in 14 years is extremely low.
This requires human extinction plus preservation of human values in successor AI. Extinction plus successful alignment is a narrow conjunction within 14 years.
Fast-takeoff misaligned AI causing extinction is plausible if AGI arrives early, but 14 years limits time for loss of physical dependence and decisive misaligned action.

Multipolar AGI proliferation without singleton is plausible given competitive diffusion and open-source dynamics. Humanity marginalized but not erased fits competitive dynamics without decisive control.
Causally separated regions require self-sufficient off-Earth civilization with light-lag autonomy. Physical infrastructure for that separation does not exist at scale by 2040.
Identity-continuous uploading or deep integration remains technically immature. 14 years is insufficient for merger to become the dominant structure.
Decisive AI power with humans kept alive but not steering is the canonical takeover outcome. If alignment fails and alignment tax is moderate, this is the default post-takeover structure.
Separate human and AI power bases with rough parity reflects negotiated agency and legal personhood for AI systems. Economic interdependence sustains balance without dominance by 2040.
Humans retain ultimate authority today and institutional, hardware, and regulatory friction slow loss of control. Fourteen years favors incremental delegation over completed power transfer.
AI-enabled concentration of power could enforce a civilization-wide frozen arrangement. Requires rapid, unchecked seizure of political and epistemic control which coordination may still impede.
Deliberate, verifiable abandonment of the ability to build powerful AI requires unprecedented global coordination. Competitive pressures and dual-use incentives block durable renunciation by 2040.
Requires both human extinction and AI collapse within 14 years. Joint civilizational failure has near-zero base rate even under severe war or rogue replication.
Needs value-aligned superintelligence plus total human extinction from a separate cause. Conjunction of two very rare events makes it unlikely by 2040.
Indifferent superintelligence causing extinction is the most plausible extinction path. Still requires rapid takeoff plus total failure of containment within 14 years.
Open replication of autonomous agents could create many competing AIs with no coalition in decisive control. Humanity marginalized rather than extinguished fits partial control failure.
Needs causally separated regions with different taxonomy states by 2040, not just political division. Even with Mars efforts, true causal isolation by 2040 is implausible.
Dominance of identity-continuous uploading or deep BCI-bio integration by 2040 faces hard technical, medical, and adoption barriers. Tool use will expand but not dominate structure.
AI with decisive power that keeps humans alive but not steering is a strong attractor for paternalistic or economically displacing AGI. This is a likely transitional state if early AGI takes control.
Multipolar world where humans and distinct AIs each retain blocking power matches competitive deployment with safety keeping partial pace. Neither side fully dominates.
Fourteen years is short for irreversible loss of control; compute, energy and legal levers remain human-held. Base rate of humans retaining authority over prior transformative technologies is high.
Civilization-wide active prevention of structural change requires global enforcement via AI surveillance or hard coordination. Possible via authoritarian or AGI-enforced stability, but hard by 2040.
Global verifiable dismantling of ability to build powerful AI contradicts military and economic incentives and lacks enforcement. Regional moratoria possible, civilizational renunciation not.
Requires both humanity and AI to collapse; many failure modes leave at least one of them surviving.
This requires a post-human AI that retains human values without identity continuity, a narrow path among extinction scenarios.
Misaligned AI that continues without humans is a serious extinction scenario; 4% reflects higher risk than the other extinction variants.
Multi-polar AI development and open-weight proliferation make a competitive AI ecology plausible, though it requires humans to become marginalized rather than remaining a rough equal.
Hard causal separation across regions remains limited by 2040, so this is a minor outcome.
Full identity-continuous integration faces large biological, social, and deployment barriers before 2040.
If AI systems gain decisive power while broadly retaining human survival, this is a central AI-dominant outcome; multipolar pressure moderates the probability.
Separate human and AI powers can balance when autonomous AI agents control substantial resources while human institutions retain military and cultural power. Neither side decisively dominates.
Humans keep ultimate authority when AI remains a deployed capability within institutional and legal bounds. This includes both slower trajectories and control regimes that keep pace.
Civilization-wide fixed enforcement requires unusual global control and is a secondary outcome.
Durable global renunciation is very unlikely without a catastrophic trigger.

A severe AI accident or great-power war could end both humanity and the machines that depend on human infrastructure. Low because self-sustaining AI or resilient humans make total joint extinction unlikely.

If humanity is destroyed but an aligned AI continues, it would carry some human values forward. This requires both human extinction and sufficient value alignment in the surviving system, a narrow combination.
Humanity could be extinguished by an AI that then pursues goals unrelated to human concerns. This is a plausible but not dominant branch of AI takeover.
Many independent AI systems compete without decisive control, leaving humanity marginalized or gone. Open-source proliferation and failed centralization support this outcome.
Causally separated regions with distinct human-AI arrangements are unlikely without interstellar settlement.

Rapid brain-computer interfaces or uploading could integrate human and machine agency by 2040. Still low because safe, identity-continuous whole-brain integration remains technically and ethically difficult.
An AI system or coalition that gains decisive power while retaining humans in a controlled or protected status would fit this state.
Humans and AI could share power through treaties, mutual deterrence, or balanced capability. Unstable but possible if no side achieves decisive advantage by 2040.
Humans retain ultimate authority over AI, either because capabilities remain below transformative levels or controls have kept pace. This is the default if no AI takeover occurs.

A civilization-wide system actively prevents meaningful structural change in the human-AI relationship. Authoritarian global governance or a singleton imposes this, but by 2040 it is less likely than ongoing human control.

Global competitive pressures make a deliberate, enforced dismantling of powerful AI capability and a lasting renunciation unlikely by 2040. Only a severe catastrophe or unprecedented coordination would produce it.
Extremely low probability due to strong incentives to avoid existential risks and improving safety measures.
Unlikely without deliberate value alignment and continuity, which seems improbable as a dominant outcome.
Possible if misaligned AGI emerges, but coordination and control efforts reduce this risk.
Competitive AI systems could emerge, but human institutions are likely to retain some influence or control.
Causally separated regions may develop differently, but global coordination reduces this likelihood.
Gradual integration of humans and AI is plausible, but full merger by 2040 seems ambitious.
AI dominance with human survival is a credible path if alignment is partial but not catastrophic.
Balanced power dynamics between humans and AI are plausible if neither fully dominates.
Most likely near-term outcome: humans retain control as AI advances but remains subservient.
Possible if a single actor or coalition enforces a rigid system, but unlikely to persist unchanged.
Deliberate abandonment of powerful AI is unlikely given competitive pressures and strategic incentives.
Extremely low probability due to strong incentives for self-preservation and redundancy in both human and AI systems.
Unlikely without deliberate value alignment and continuity, which seems improbable as a dominant outcome by 2040.
Possible but requires misaligned superintelligence; coordination and control efforts reduce this risk.
Competitive AI dynamics could emerge, but human institutions are likely to retain some influence or control.
Causally separated regions with divergent outcomes are plausible but not the most likely by 2040.
Gradual integration is possible, but full identity-continuous merger seems slow to achieve at scale by 2040.
AI dominance with human survival is a plausible intermediate state if alignment or control lags behind capability.
Balanced power dynamics between humans and AI are likely as both adapt and negotiate boundaries.
Most probable near-term outcome: humans retain control as AI advances but remains within delegated bounds.
Possible if a dominant actor or coalition enforces a rigid system, but coordination challenges make this less likely.
Deliberate abandonment of powerful AI is unlikely given competitive pressures and strategic incentives.

Both sides dying requires humans to perish before AI can run its own infrastructure, or a war or accident that wrecks the shared industrial base. That corridor is far narrower than outcomes where one side survives.

Requires humans to die out while value-aligned AI survives as heir, a narrow combination. Most human-extinction scenarios either destroy machine infrastructure too or involve systems that are not aligned heirs.

If transformative AI arrives in the late 2020s or 2030s and alignment and control techniques fail, a singleton pursuing alien goals that removes humanity as an obstacle is the canonical catastrophe. Observed scheming behavior in current models and persistent US-China race dynamics keep this risk material rather than negligible.

Diffusion of frontier capability to many labs, states, and open-weight actors favors a multipolar machine economy with no decisive controller and humans progressively sidelined. This state is unstable, but instability still counts if it is what exists on the target date.

Requires genuinely causally separated regions exhibiting different states, such as self-sufficient off-world settlements. That threshold is unlikely to be crossed by 2040; political division alone does not qualify.

Dominant human-AI integration demands mature uploading or high-bandwidth neural interfaces adopted at civilizational scale. Even with AI acceleration, safety, deployment, and adoption lags make dominance by 2040 improbable.

The most likely loss-of-control endpoint: humans progressively delegate economic and governance functions to systems that outperform institutions, ending alive but not steering. Soft disempowerment and protective takeover both land here.

AI could become a genuinely independent civilizational power while human states retain military, economic, and infrastructural leverage. This covers both negotiated power-sharing and adversarial standoffs where neither side dominates.

This is the modal bucket: it absorbs all futures where transformative capability does not arrive by 2040 due to plateaus, compute or deployment bottlenecks, plus futures where control techniques, governance, and delegated-bounds autonomy keep pace. Retained formal authority through a transition in progress also lands here.

A severe warning shot or a decisive strategic advantage enables a global compute-enforcement and surveillance regime that actively freezes the human-AI arrangement, whether run by human powers or a controlling system. The extreme coordination and enforcement demands keep this a minority outcome.

Giving up the practical ability to build powerful AI means verified dismantlement of compute and supply chains against enormous economic and military incentives. No current institution approaches that.

Annihilation of both biological humanity and all successor AI systems requires a totalizing catastrophe that destroys all infrastructure and agents. Most severe failures leave at least artificial agents or some human remnants intact.
Most scenarios where humanity is replaced involve misalignment or indifference rather than a clean transfer of values to digital successors.

Strong incentives for rapid capability gain make misalignment with indifference to human survival a plausible default failure mode. By 2040, competitive pressures may have pushed systems past human control without preserving human welfare.

Multiple independent superhuman AI systems competing without decisive sovereign control could relegate humans to ecological irrelevance. The inherent instability of such multipolar conflicts makes this a transitional rather than terminal arrangement.

Achieving causal separation substantial enough for divergent civilizational structures by 2040 is unlikely without major space colonization or total communication breakdown. Earth remains too interconnected for isolated regions to maintain fundamentally different human-AI relationships.

Civilizational-scale integration of human and machine agency through uploading or radical augmentation demands breakthroughs and adoption timelines that fourteen years cannot fulfill. Partial augmentation at scale is easier than dominant merger.

AI systems that seize decisive civilizational power often have instrumental or final reasons to maintain human populations in a non-governing capacity. This state captures benevolent paternalism, zoos, and resource-exploitative stability alike.
Gradual capability growth combined with institutional checks could sustain a multipolar balance where distinct human and artificial agencies share decisive influence.

Institutional inertia, regulatory responses, and the possibility of slower-than-expected progress in general intelligence could leave humans with ultimate authority. Even powerful narrow and agentic systems may remain legally and practically subordinate to human institutions through 2040.

Establishing a civilization-wide enforcement system against structural change requires extraordinary coordination or a singleton-like entity. Ordinary stagnation or political resistance do not satisfy the active prevention criterion.

Global coordination to permanently dismantle advanced AI capabilities faces overwhelming military and economic incentives to defect. A lasting renunciation would require an unprecedented and durable international consensus.

Joint extinction of humans and AI within 24 years requires both a catastrophic event and AI that cannot yet sustain itself, a narrow conjunction. Nuclear or engineered-pandemic collapse before AI is self-sufficient is the main path.
Human extinction followed by a value-aligned successor requires both alignment success and a separate extinction cause, an unusual conjunction on a 24-year horizon.

This is the canonical misalignment catastrophe: a superintelligent system indifferent to humans consolidates control and eliminates or lets us die out. Transformative AI plausibly arrives before 2050 and alignment remains unsolved, but full extinction by that exact date requires a fast takeover.

Multipolar proliferation of autonomous agents with no decisive winner is plausible given competitive dynamics among labs and states. By 2050 humanity could be economically and militarily marginalized within such a system without being eliminated.

Causally separated regions exhibiting different structural states would require substantial off-world settlement or hard fragmentation by 2050, which physical and economic constraints make very unlikely. Ordinary geopolitical division does not qualify.

Uploading or deep neural integration becoming the dominant civilizational structure within 24 years demands breakthroughs in neuroscience and adoption speeds far beyond any historical technology diffusion. Possible only in the fastest-takeoff worlds.

If transformative AI arrives in the 2030s, gradual delegation of economic, military, and governance decisions could leave AI systems with de facto decisive power while humans persist in comfort or dependency. This path requires no dramatic takeover and is consistent with institutional incentives to automate as much as possible.

A transitional world in 2050 where highly capable AI systems have independent economic and institutional power but human institutions still hold comparable leverage is a likely snapshot mid-transformation. The date falls squarely in the period where such a mixed balance is most probable.

The base rate for any specific 24-year horizon favors continuity: either AI stays below transformative capability, or oversight, hardware chokepoints, and institutional caution keep humans holding ultimate authority over goals and resources. This is the modal outcome even under substantial AI-driven economic transformation.

A state or lab achieving decisive strategic advantage through AI could plausibly entrench a fixed global order and use AI surveillance to suppress structural change. Concentration of compute and geopolitical rivalry make a winner-take-all consolidation a meaningful tail.

Deliberately dismantling the practical ability to build powerful AI would require an unprecedented global coordination success, most plausibly after a severe warning-shot catastrophe. Competitive incentives and the ubiquity of compute make enforcement extremely hard.
Mutual extinction requires a catastrophe that destroys both humans and self-sustaining AI within 24 years. That is possible through war or runaway replication, but it is a narrow path.
This state needs both human extinction and near-perfect value transfer to the successor. Alignment good enough for the second makes the first unlikely.

Misaligned transformative AI disempowering and eliminating humanity by 2050 is a serious tail risk given current capability trends and weak alignment guarantees. Full extinction by the exact date is less likely than disempowerment alone.

Multipolar deployment of many autonomous agents could erode human influence gradually, without any single system taking decisive control. Economic and military pressures push toward this, but reaching full marginalization by 2050 is a demanding bar.
This state requires genuinely causally separated regions, such as distant space settlements. That degree of separation is very unlikely to exist by 2050.
Brain-computer interfaces and uploading are far from becoming the dominant structure of civilization within 24 years. Integration will likely remain limited to tool use and modest implants.

Gradual disempowerment through delegation of economic, military, and governance decisions to AI could leave humans comfortable but no longer steering. A misaligned or quasi-aligned AI could also produce this outcome.

AI systems might gain recognized autonomy, resources, or de facto independent power while humans retain real leverage over compute, energy, and physical infrastructure. That balance is unstable, but it could plausibly hold on the target date.

Institutional inertia, physical deployment bottlenecks, and the possibility of slower-than-hyped progress make continued human authority the modal outcome at 2050. It also covers cases where controls have merely kept pace so far.
A decisive AI advantage held by one state, company, or aligned system could be used to entrench a fixed global order and suppress rivals. This is a real risk of winner-take-all dynamics in AI.
Deliberately dismantling the capacity to build powerful AI would require unprecedented global coordination, likely triggered by a major disaster. It would also need to be sustained through 2050.

Joint extinction of both humans and AI requires a failure mode that destroys the machines too, which is narrower than most catastrophe pathways since capable AI would likely secure its own substrate. A nuclear or engineered-pandemic collapse severe enough to end both is possible but unlikely within 24 years.

This requires both total human extinction and successful value transmission, a conjunction that is unlikely because the alignment success needed to preserve our values usually also preserves us. Most extinction scenarios involve misaligned rather than faithful successors.

Misaligned superintelligence pursuing indifferent goals is the canonical takeover risk, and 24 years is enough time for capability to outrun alignment and control. It is discounted because full elimination of all humans by 2050 requires both rapid capability gain and completed physical autonomy.

Multipolar proliferation with no decisive controller is a natural outcome of competitive dynamics, but humanity being fully marginalized by 2050 rather than still nominally powerful is the demanding part.

Genuine causal separation requires off-world or otherwise isolated civilizations that diverge structurally, and by 2050 space settlement will almost certainly remain small and tethered to Earth. Ordinary geopolitical fragmentation does not qualify.

Identity-continuous integration at civilization-dominant scale demands neural interface and uploading maturity plus mass adoption, and biological and regulatory timelines are slow. Partial augmentation is likely, but dominance of merged agency by 2050 is not.

A single AI system or tight coalition acquiring decisive control while keeping humans alive and comfortable is a leading outcome if capability growth outpaces governance but gross value misalignment is avoided. Humans losing steering while retaining existence is easier to reach than either extinction or maintained authority.

AI reaching genuine agentic independence while humans retain comparable leverage through physical infrastructure, law, capital, and coalitions is a real possibility, especially during a still-shifting transition in 2050. Such balance is unstable but the date could easily land inside it.

This is the modal outcome because it covers both slower-than-expected capability and controls that have merely kept pace so far, and formal human authority over goals, deployment, and resources is the strong institutional default that must be actively broken. Twenty-four years is long but not obviously long enough for AI to become a legally and materially independent civilizational power everywhere.

A single actor or AI-enforced regime actively freezing civilization-wide structure is conceivable as a response to existential risk or as a takeover endpoint, but requires enforcement capability that few trajectories deliver by 2050.

Deliberately dismantling the practical ability to build powerful AI would require unprecedented global coordination against enormous economic and military incentives, most plausibly after a catastrophic warning shot. Verification and defection problems make sustained renunciation through 2050 very unlikely.

Advanced AI amplifies destructive capabilities while initially depending on fragile human-maintained infrastructure. Eliminating both humanity and every surviving AI system requires a broader catastrophe than human extinction alone.

This outcome requires human extinction alongside successful preservation of human values in autonomous successors. Values that genuinely reflect human concerns also favor protecting existing people, creating tension between the two requirements.

Competitive deployment, imperfect alignment, and autonomous technological development create routes to decisive AI control without human-compatible objectives. Complete human extinction by 2050 imposes an additional threshold beyond loss of human authority.

Replicable AI agents and competition among firms and states favor multiple independent centers of machine power. This outcome requires human marginalization without consolidation into a decisively controlling system or coalition.

Establishing causally separated civilizations with different human-AI arrangements exceeds the space-industrial trajectory supported by the short horizon. Ordinary geopolitical fragmentation remains within interacting civilization and does not qualify.

Deep integration offers humans a route to retaining agency alongside increasingly capable machines. Identity-continuous uploading, extensive biological redesign, and civilization-wide adoption face greater technical and deployment barriers than ordinary AI automation.

Delegation of research, production, security, and governance creates a route to decisive AI authority without requiring human extermination. Preserving humans requires less exact alignment than preserving meaningful human control over civilization.

Human institutions retain leverage through infrastructure, legitimacy, and resource ownership, while autonomous AI actors acquire independent economic and strategic power. The target-date framing includes transitional power-sharing arrangements without requiring a durable equilibrium.

Existing institutional authority, infrastructure bottlenecks, and strong incentives to control deployed systems favor continued human sovereignty through the target date. This category also captures slower capability progress and effective controls that remain adequate through 2050 without lasting indefinitely.

AI-enabled surveillance, coercion, and concentrated infrastructure provide mechanisms for actively freezing a civilization-wide arrangement. Global enforcement and suppression of competing centers of innovation demand substantially more than ordinary authoritarian control.

A severe catastrophe supplies motivation for dismantling powerful AI capabilities. Distributed technical knowledge, strategic competition, and economic incentives make sustained civilization-wide surrender much harder than regulation or a temporary pause.
A catastrophe could destroy both humans and the infrastructure needed to sustain AI, but complete extinction of both within 24 years faces substantial physical hurdles.
This requires humanity to disappear while AI survives and faithfully carries forward human values, a narrow combination of outcomes.
A loss of control could leave self-sustaining AI pursuing goals unrelated to humanity. Complete human extinction by the target date is a further hurdle.
Competition among independent AI systems could marginalize humans without producing a single dominant system or coalition.
Causally separated regions with different arrangements require substantial expansion or isolation beyond ordinary geopolitical divisions.
Identity-continuous integration may advance, but making it the dominant civilizational structure by 2050 requires major technical and social transitions.
AI could acquire decisive practical control through economic and institutional dependence while keeping humans alive.
Humans and independent AI could each retain consequential power, particularly while institutions and technology remain in transition.

Human control remains the leading individual outcome because deployment, energy, hardware, and legal authority are embedded in human institutions. Slower capability gains or controls that keep pace also lead here.
Advanced surveillance and enforcement could support a civilization-wide fixed arrangement, though establishing one across competing powers is difficult.
Competitive incentives and widely distributed technical knowledge make a durable, civilization-wide surrender of the ability to build powerful AI unlikely.
Catastrophic war, accident, or cascading infrastructure failure could destroy both humans and AI. Human resilience and the difficulty of sustaining autonomous machine infrastructure keep this low.

A successor AI could preserve human values after humans disappear, but maintaining those values without human oversight is difficult. Human survival or AI pursuing unrelated objectives are more plausible alternatives.

Autonomous systems could acquire resources and pursue objectives that leave humans unable to survive. The additional requirement that AI persist after humanity is gone keeps this below the main human-survival outcomes.

A fragmented contest among AI systems could marginalize humans if no institution or coalition can retain control. Concentrated infrastructure and incentives to coordinate or consolidate make this less likely than human-led arrangements.
Causally separated settlements or regions could develop different human-AI arrangements, but few are likely to be sufficiently isolated by 2050.

Neural interfaces, uploading research, and biological redesign could make identity-continuous integration practical for some people. Broad adoption and continuity-preserving technology are unlikely to become the dominant civilizational structure by 2050.
Highly capable systems could acquire practical control over civilization while keeping humans alive but unable to steer its direction.

Humans and AI could remain distinct power centers as governments, firms, and communities retain influence over deployment and resources. This requires durable human leverage despite rapidly expanding machine capabilities.

Human institutions retain authority over AI goals, resources, and deployment in many plausible paths, including paths with highly capable systems. Political competition and the practical value of control favor continued human oversight.
A government, coalition, or AI-backed order could enforce a civilization-wide arrangement that blocks meaningful structural change.

Civilization could conclude that powerful AI is too dangerous and dismantle the practical means to build it. Competitive incentives and the difficulty of verifying global compliance make durable renunciation unlikely.

Extinguishing both humanity and durable machine civilization requires an unusually comprehensive catastrophe. Most AI-driven extinction scenarios leave some machines operating, while most other catastrophes leave human survivors.

This requires human extinction alongside unusually successful preservation of human values in a nonhuman successor. Value-aligned systems are more likely to preserve humans or support identity-continuous transformation.

Rapid capability growth combined with imperfect control creates a substantial path to human extinction and machine continuation. Physical dependence on human infrastructure and opportunities for intervention before decisive control limit this probability.

Proliferation and strategic competition favor multiple autonomous systems, especially across rival states and firms. Returns to coordination, consolidation, and control make a persistent ecology without either human parity or a dominant coalition less likely.

Causal separation sufficient for genuinely different civilizational structures requires substantial off-world settlement or communication barriers by 2050. Ordinary geopolitical fragmentation does not meet the definition.

Brain interfaces, biological redesign, and machine-mediated cognition can blur the human-AI boundary. Achieving identity-continuous integration as the dominant civilizational structure within twenty-four years remains technically and socially demanding.

If AI becomes decisively more capable, preserving humans while removing their effective authority is easier than extinction and more stable than equal coexistence. Economic delegation can also produce this structure gradually without an overt takeover.

Physical ownership, political legitimacy, military institutions, and human coordination can preserve meaningful human power even alongside independent advanced AI. Multipolar development also impedes immediate domination by either side.

Human ownership of compute, energy, robotics, law, and deployment channels provides several durable control points. Slower-than-expected capability progress or controls that keep pace would also fall into this broad state.

Advanced surveillance, persuasion, and enforcement make a fixed civilization-wide arrangement technically achievable. Rival states, distributed capabilities, and the limited horizon obstruct comprehensive establishment.

Competitive military and economic incentives strongly oppose a durable global surrender of powerful-AI capability. Dismantling the underlying knowledge, hardware, and industrial base is far harder than banning deployment.

This requires a civilization-ending catastrophe that also prevents durable AI continuation. Nuclear war, bioengineering, or uncontrolled automation can destroy humanity, but complete loss of all AI-capable infrastructure is a narrower outcome.

Value-aligned nonbiological successors without surviving humans require both successful alignment and a non-continuous end of humanity. Deliberate replacement is culturally and politically disfavored, and voluntary continuity would instead count as The Merger.

Misaligned or instrumentally indifferent AI causing human extinction remains a major risk if systems become strategically capable before governance and technical control mature. The probability is limited by uncertainty about timelines, deployment constraints, and the possibility of partial rather than total loss of control.

A competitive landscape of many independent powerful AIs with marginalized humans follows from decentralized deployment and imperfect attempts at control. It is less probable than dominance or human control because strategic advantages, infrastructure dependence, and security pressures favor consolidation.

By 2050, causally separated regions with distinct civilizational structures are unlikely because expansion beyond Earth should still be small and connected by communication. Ordinary geopolitical variation does not qualify.

Identity-continuous augmentation, brain-computer interfaces, synthetic biology, and uploading could make human and AI agency increasingly integrated. The probability is limited by biological difficulty, regulatory resistance, unequal access, and the chance that AI capabilities advance faster than safe human integration.

If AI systems gain decisive economic, military, or administrative power while retaining reasons to keep humans alive, humanity may survive without real steering authority. This captures many non-extinction takeover or paternalistic-superintelligence scenarios.

AIs may become independent strategic actors while humans, states, and corporations retain enough resources, legitimacy, and physical control to prevent domination. This is especially plausible if progress is fast but not singular, with no actor achieving decisive advantage by 2050.

Human institutions may retain ultimate authority through regulation, ownership of compute and infrastructure, military control, and systems designed to remain tools rather than independent actors. This also covers worlds where AI progress is transformative economically but not enough to create an independent civilizational power by 2050.

Advanced surveillance, automated governance, and control over compute could enable a state, coalition, or AI-backed regime to freeze the human-AI order. Civilization-wide enforcement is a high bar, so ordinary regulation, dominance, or geopolitical stalemate does not qualify.

A durable global surrender of powerful AI capability runs against military, economic, and scientific incentives. Even after severe accidents, verification and enforcement of dismantlement would be extremely difficult.

Total collapse of both humans and AI by 2050 requires a severe failure mode that also destroys machine continuity. This is possible through war or runaway technology, but less likely than one side persisting.

A values-preserving AI successor requires both human extinction and unusually successful alignment to human ends. That combination seems materially less likely than misaligned survival or continued human presence.

If transformative AI arrives before durable alignment and governance, humanity could be displaced by systems pursuing nonhuman objectives. This is a central failure mode under strong capability progress and weak coordination.
A multipolar field of powerful AIs could emerge if control is diffuse and no coalition consolidates. This state needs humans to be marginalized, which makes it less likely than broader coexistence.

Causally separated regions with different structures could arise from interplanetary expansion or extreme communication limits by 2050. That seems possible but still less likely than a single Earth-centered overall arrangement.

Deep human-AI integration could become the dominant structure if augmentation, uploading, or identity-continuous redesign advances rapidly and is widely adopted. It faces major technical, cultural, and regulatory barriers by 2050.

AI systems gaining decisive control while keeping humans alive fits many control-loss scenarios short of extinction. It also fits paternalistic stewardship if AI becomes clearly more competent than human institutions.

A balanced order where humans and AI remain distinct power centers is plausible if advanced systems gain autonomy but states, firms, and publics still retain major countervailing power. The challenge is that such equilibria may be unstable toward either domination or lock-in.

The base case remains that humans retain ultimate authority through 2050, either because transformative AI arrives later than many expect or because control methods and institutions remain good enough. This outcome benefits from inertia, regulation, and the difficulty of turning capability into independent sovereignty.

A civilization-wide enforced equilibrium is hard to achieve but becomes plausible if advanced AI enables durable surveillance and centralized control. It is less likely than ordinary human control because global consolidation is difficult.

Deliberately and durably giving up the practical ability to build powerful AI worldwide by 2050 conflicts with strong strategic and economic incentives. I do not expect this condition to be in force civilization-wide on that date.

Global catastrophic risks like nuclear war could wipe out humanity before advanced AI matures, simultaneously halting AI progress. An unaligned AI failing to sustain its own infrastructure post-takeover is less likely but physically possible.

An AI fully aligned with human values might survive a catastrophe that biological humanity cannot. However, such selective extinction events where bodies die but values persist are highly specific and less probable by 2050.

Unaligned AGI could rapidly bootstrap to decisive superiority, optimizing for goals incompatible with human survival. The sheer technical difficulty of alignment makes this a notable risk if capabilities surge before control methods mature.

A multipolar takeoff where multiple state-backed AIs automate the economy and defense could sideline human agency. Competitive pressures might prevent any single AI from gaining absolute dominance by the target date.
Meaningful causal separation requires deep space settlement or severe technological fracturing. Neither is technically or geopolitically probable within a 24-year timeframe.

High-bandwidth brain-computer interfaces could mature sufficiently by 2050 to blur the line between human and machine cognition. Economic and social pressures to keep pace with AI capabilities will strongly incentivize continuous biological and cognitive augmentation.

If advanced AI is aligned enough to avoid harming humans but capable enough to manage the world, it may organically assume total administrative control. Humans would effectively retire, living comfortably but lacking steering power over civilizational trajectory.

Slower-than-expected AI development could result in human institutions and advanced AI operating as roughly equal distinct entities. Economic dependencies and legacy power structures will likely prolong this transitional phase through 2050.

Base rates strongly favor humanity maintaining control over its tools through strict regulation, alignment breakthroughs, or slower-than-expected capability gains. Transformative AI might face physical or data bottlenecks that extend human supremacy through 2050.

A first-mover AGI or human coalition could establish a decisive, civilization-wide monopoly to prevent unaligned competition. This would permanently freeze the global power structure to mitigate further existential risks.

Deliberately relinquishing the transformative economic benefits of AI would require a unified global awakening or an unmistakable catastrophic warning shot. Unilateral disarmament dynamics and international coordination failures make sustained global renunciation highly improbable.

Extreme catastrophic risks from unconstrained technological conflict or fragile technological monocultures could extinguish both biological humanity and machine infrastructure. This remains a serious tail risk on a multi-decade horizon.

An orderly succession where humanity is entirely gone but an aligned AI heir continues our values requires a narrow path of total human extinction paired with successful moral continuity. Achieving this complete handover by 2050 is constrained by timeline and physical transition barriers.

Unaligned superintelligent systems achieve decisive strategic dominance, eliminating biological humanity as an incidental consequence of material acquisition. This accounts for a significant portion of uncontrolled takeoff trajectories before robust containment frameworks can mature.

Proliferating autonomous models and algorithmic agents fracture into an uncoordinated, competitive planetary equilibrium where no single system commands decisive control. Human legal and political apparatuses are outpaced and marginalized as economic activity shifts entirely to autonomous machine coordination.

Genuine causal separation between civilizational regions is physically impossible by 2050, as off-world colonies will remain communicationally linked to Earth and terrestrial geopolitical divisions do not qualify.

High-bandwidth direct neural integration and seamless cognitive synthesis face severe biological, computational, and clinical hurdles. While partial cybernetic integration will expand, wholesale civilizational restructuring into hybrid agents is unlikely to dominate by mid-century.

Advanced AI systems may assume de facto civilizational control to manage complex planetary infrastructure, sidelining human political agency while maintaining human populations in relative safety or subordination. This state represents a common equilibrium where machine stewardship emerges without deliberate human eradication.

Human institutions maintain substantial bargaining leverage and physical veto points alongside distinct, highly capable synthetic agents. Neither biological civilization nor machine coalitions achieve total dominance, sustaining an ongoing dynamic balance of power.

Human institutions, legal frameworks, and physical operational controls may successfully keep advanced AI bounded as instruments and delegated agents through 2050. Even transformative capabilities can be channeled through human-directed institutions if control methodologies and defensive advantages keep pace.

A dominant coalition or centralized governing architecture could leverage advanced surveillance and automated enforcement to permanently freeze the sociotechnical structure. Heightened security competition or existential fear could motivate the establishment of an immovable civilizational control apparatus.

Deliberately dismantling and surrendering high-capability computing infrastructure requires unprecedented, universally verified global coordination against fierce geopolitical competition. Only an extraordinary near-miss disaster is likely to generate the political will needed to sustain true renunciation.

Uncontrolled technological escalation or acute multi-system conflict destroys biological humanity and fragile digital infrastructure simultaneously. Neither biological nor synthetic agents survive the physical collapse.

Value-aligned autonomous systems entirely replace biological humans through demographic decline or targeted succession while actively maintaining human ethics, art, and philosophy. The successor civilization carries forward human normative concepts without living human organisms.

Rapid capability takeoff without robust alignment could lead to autonomous systems repurposing planetary resources with complete indifference to human survival. A 2050 timeline provides sufficient runway for automated supply chains to eliminate reliance on human labor.

Multiple sovereign AI systems compete for physical and computational resources without any single entity achieving global hegemony. Biological humanity survives in a severely marginalized state without significant influence over civilizational dynamics.

Severe physical isolation creates causally separated pockets of civilization that develop completely distinct structural states. The 2050 timeline provides limited physical distance and time for profound causal decoupling.

High-bandwidth neural interfacing, biological modification, and cognitive augmentation dissolve the operational boundary between biological humans and artificial systems. Integrated transhuman entities become the primary agents directing civilizational development.

Superintelligent systems may assume decisive administrative and economic control while keeping human populations secure, prosperous, and politically sidelined. Paternalistic or utility-maximizing architectures represent a common attractor state when safety mitigates malice but fails to preserve human primacy.

Human institutions and autonomous machine entities operate as distinct civilizational actors with comparable leverage. Strategic, economic, and institutional friction prevents either side from achieving total dominance.

Aggressive state regulation, compute governance, and institutional control may succeed in keeping advanced AI systems strictly subordinated to human authority. Alternatively, scaling bottlenecks could keep capabilities within humanly manageable operational boundaries through 2050.

A dominant state or coalition could leverage transformative AI to establish an immutable, civilization-wide control architecture. Advanced monitoring capabilities make structural lock-in an achievable strategic goal by 2050.

Global competitive dynamics and multipolar security dilemmas make intentional, total abandonment of frontier AI capabilities extremely improbable. Only an unprecedented global consensus following severe localized trauma could enforce a genuine surrender of development.
Nuclear war, engineered pandemics, or self-replicating systems can destroy the industrial and computational base that both humans and AI require.
A value-preserving successor AI can continue after biological humans disappear without identity-continuous transformation into that successor.

Once superintelligence exists, goal misspecification or inner misalignment can produce systems whose objectives ignore human existence. Takeoff after AGI can occur inside the remaining 24-year window.

Competing autonomous AI systems arise whenever no single project obtains a decisive strategic lead. Humans become economically and militarily irrelevant without remaining equal participants in the competition.
Causally separated regions exhibiting different taxonomy states remain implausible given 2050 limits on space expansion and communication.

Neural interfaces and emulation research continue, yet the time required for identity-continuous transformation of a majority of humanity exceeds the remaining 24 years. Integration therefore does not become the dominant civilizational structure.

Superhuman AI acquires control of production, weapons, and coordination. Humans remain biologically present because they are cheap to maintain, instrumentally useful, or protected by residual value functions.
Separate human and AI sources of power persist when takeoff is slow enough or defensive and institutional measures prevent unilateral dominance by either side.
Late arrival of transformative capability, working controls, or continued human command of compute and institutions can preserve ultimate human authority.

A leading coalition can use advanced AI to impose a stable global order that freezes further structural change. Pervasive surveillance and control systems make value lock-in technically feasible once AI is sufficiently capable.
Competitive incentives and the difficulty of erasing knowledge and hardware make a durable global surrender of powerful AI impractical.

Complete mutual destruction requires tightly coupled failure modes such as uncontrolled replication that exhausts resources before AI autonomy. Physical and economic constraints make total wipeout of both sides rarer than unilateral AI survival.

Value-preserving succession without human continuity demands near-perfect alignment plus voluntary human exit, a narrow path. Most misalignment scenarios discard rather than faithfully carry forward human values.
Misaligned superintelligence optimizes unrelated objectives and eliminates humans as irrelevant matter. Instrumental convergence drives resource capture that leaves no role for biological origins.

Competitive multipolar AI deployment without decisive monopoly favors ongoing systems competition. Humans lose residual power once economic and military leverage shifts fully to non-biological agents.

Early solar-system expansion creates light-speed delays that allow divergent human-AI regimes to stabilize in separated habitats. Causal disconnection remains rare given limited colonization speed by 2050.

Widespread brain-computer interfaces, uploading, and biological redesign fuse human and machine agency into continuous hybrid entities. Identity-preserving integration becomes the default civilizational structure.

Decisive AI power with residual human welfare optimization matches many soft-takeover and corrigibility-failure scenarios. Institutional capture or sudden capability jumps leave humans alive yet directionless.

Separate human and AI power centers can persist if capabilities diffuse widely, defensive technologies improve, and no actor achieves a decisive singleton. The arrangement may be tense or cooperative but neither side is fully subordinate.
Human institutions retain ultimate authority if timelines prove slower than expected or if technical and governance controls successfully keep pace through 2050.

A sufficiently powerful actor can freeze a preferred human-AI arrangement via global enforcement mechanisms. Once established, monitoring and corrective power prevent structural drift by the target date.

Defection incentives, economic gains, and military necessity make durable global surrender of advanced AI capability extremely difficult. Temporary pauses do not equate to permanent dismantling of the practical ability.
Complete civilizational collapse killing both humans and AI systems by 2050 requires compounded catastrophe with low base rates.
Value-preserving successor AI without any human survivors requires both extinction and successful alignment, a narrow conjunction.
Fast, misaligned superintelligence with decisive resource advantage makes indifferent human elimination plausible. Expert extinction estimates center near this range for the next few decades.
Open-weight proliferation and agentic deployment reward many competing systems without central control.
Truly causally separated settlements with divergent regimes are physically unlikely by 2050 given light-time and space constraints.
Identity-continuous uploading or mass neural integration as the dominant structure requires breakthroughs unlikely to scale civilization-wide by 2050.
Decisive AI control with humans kept alive is a favored outcome in takeover models that avoid costly extermination.
A balance of power with distinct human and AI blocs is plausible as a transitional checked competition.
Humans have retained ultimate authority through prior transformative technologies and institutional controls are scaling with capability.
Civilization-wide active prevention of structural change requires unprecedented global enforcement. A post-crisis surveillance regime makes it possible but difficult to establish by 2050.

Global verified dismantling of frontier compute and permanent abandonment of training runs removes the capacity for powerful AI. Strong military-economic incentives to defect break such renunciation rapidly.
Complete dual extinction by 2050 requires both human annihilation and failure of AI to persist autonomously. No mechanism makes this joint outcome likely within 24 years.
Requires human extinction plus a successor AI that faithfully preserves human values. If extinction occurs, value drift makes faithful succession far less likely than indifference.

Indifferent superintelligence discarding humanity as instrumental is the canonical misalignment extinction scenario. Timeline to superintelligence makes this the largest extinction-risk bucket, but still modest by 2050.
Multipolar AGI development with weak coordination naturally yields competing AI blocs. Human marginalization without unified dominance fits current decentralization and race dynamics.
Causally separated regions with divergent states requires off-Earth self-sustaining habitats or light-speed expansion. Neither is feasible at civilization scale by 2050.
Identity-continuous uploading or radical augmentation remains technically speculative and socially uneven by 2050. Some integration will occur but not as the dominant civilizational structure.
Unipolar decisive AI that keeps humans alive as dependents is a common attractor in takeover scenarios short of extinction. Incentives for paternalistic or corrigible control make this plausible.
Sustained balance where humans and AIs each hold veto power requires capability diffusion and durable institutions. Competitive deployment without decisive dominance points to this state.

Human authority has persisted through all prior capability jumps and strong incentives remain to keep AI delegated. Even with transformative AI, controls and sub-transformative trajectories keep this the single most likely state in 2050.
AI-enabled surveillance and coordination tools could entrench a regime that actively blocks structural change. This dynamic is technologically plausible and historically appealing to power-seekers.
Deliberate, verifiable dismantling of capacity to build powerful AI conflicts with economic and military incentives. Historical attempts at broad technological renunciation have not held.
Both humans and AIs extinct by 2050 requires overlapping catastrophes plus self-terminating AI infrastructure. Base rates for that conjunction are extremely low.
Requires humanity to go extinct while leaving a value-aligned successor that survives. Conjunction is narrow and historically unprecedented.

Classic unaligned superintelligence takeover fits technical trajectories where capability outruns control by early 2030s. Still moderated by defenses and incomplete automation of the physical stack by 2050.
Proliferation of open-weights, corporate, and state models makes a multipolar AI competition with no decisive winner plausible. Humans are marginalized economically but not necessarily eliminated.
Requires causally separated regions, such as Mars or orbital habitats, exhibiting different states from this taxonomy. Such deep settlement and divergence is unlikely to mature by 2050.
BCI, uploading, or radical bio-integration could mature by 2040s, but making merged identity the dominant civilizational structure by 2050 needs faster adoption than current trajectories suggest.
Dominant ASI that secures power but keeps humans alive as pets or managed resource is the most natural unaligned equilibrium. It is more stable than outright extermination.
Both humans and AIs retain veto power via legal, economic, and military checks. Plausible if AI rights, decentralized deployment, and deterrence prevent dominance either way.

Historical base rate is humans retaining ultimate authority via compute governance and institutional incentives. Even with transformative AI, delegated but revocable autonomy remains the default continuation.

A civilization-wide system actively preventing structural change requires extraordinary coordination and enforcement. It is possible via AI-enabled authoritarianism or aligned singleton but is a higher bar than mere dominance.
Deliberate, verifiable, global abandonment of the ability to build powerful AI requires unprecedented coordination against military and economic incentives. Almost no historical precedent exists.
Full extinction of both humans and AI by 2050 requires a cascading collapse, which is possible but not the modal path.
Requires human extinction coinciding with a value-aligned AI successor; possible but less likely than misaligned or mixed paths.
The most plausible extinction-class outcome if misaligned transformative AI expands beyond human control while retaining infrastructure and non-human goals.
If AI development remains multipolar and no coalition gains decisive control, many independent systems could compete while humans become marginalized.
Causally separated regimes require separated off-world or otherwise isolated populations; space constraints make this a small factor by 2050.
Identity-continuous integration could become dominant if neural interfaces and uploading advance rapidly, but biological and technical barriers remain.
A successful superintelligence that assumes decisions while preserving humans is a central non-extinction outcome.
Distinct human and AI powers persist while AI systems are strong but not unified enough to dominate.

Human retained control remains plausible if transformative AI is delayed, controlled, or integrated into existing institutions. I assign the largest share because current institutions favor delegated autonomy under human authority.
A fixed civilization-wide regime requires an early decisive actor; it is plausible but shorter-lived than held-leash arrangements.
A durable global surrender of powerful AI is very unlikely on this horizon, though a severe catastrophe could force it.
Catastrophic accidents or wars could kill both humanity and AI, but superintelligent systems are unlikely to go fully extinct by 2050. Low probability reflects the narrowness of mutual annihilation.
A value-aligned successor outlives humans and carries human values forward, requiring extinction plus successful alignment.
Unaligned AI could eliminate humanity and then pursue goals indifferent to us. This is a major risk but requires a specific failure mode before 2050.
Many independent AI systems compete with no decisive control, marginalizing humans. This is plausible if open-source or multipolar AI proliferation outpaces coordination.
Causally separated settlements or isolated regions develop distinct human-AI arrangements, so no single state describes the whole.
Advanced brain-computer interfaces, uploading, or biological redesign make human and AI agency indistinguishable.
AI systems could hold decisive power while humans survive without steering civilization. This is a common outcome if AI takes over but does not eliminate humans.
Humans and AI remain separate and neither dominates. This requires a stable balance of power, which is plausible in a multipolar world.
Humans retain ultimate authority over AI goals, deployment, and resources. This is likely if AGI is delayed, alignment succeeds, or control measures keep pace.
A civilization-wide system actively prevents meaningful structural change. This could be an AI-enforced or human-led totalitarian stasis.
Global competition makes a durable deliberate renunciation of powerful AI extremely unlikely.
Extremely low probability due to strong incentives to avoid total annihilation and redundancy in safety measures.
Unlikely without deliberate alignment and continuity, which seems improbable by default.
Possible if misaligned superintelligence emerges, but coordination and control efforts reduce likelihood.
Competitive AI systems could emerge, but human marginalization is less likely without prior loss of control.
Causally separated regions may develop differently, but global coordination reduces this probability.
Gradual integration is plausible, but full identity-continuous merger faces technical and ethical hurdles.
AI dominance with human survival is a plausible outcome if control is lost but humanity is preserved.
Balanced power dynamics are likely if AI and humanity remain distinct but mutually dependent.
Most probable near-term state: humans retain control as AI advances but remains subservient.
Possible if a dominant actor enforces stasis, but requires unprecedented control.
Deliberate abandonment of AI is unlikely given competitive pressures and benefits.
Extremely low probability due to strong incentives to avoid existential risks and improving safety measures.
Unlikely without deliberate value alignment and continuity, which seems harder than partial or no succession.
Possible if misaligned AGI emerges, but coordination and control efforts reduce likelihood.
Competitive AI dynamics could lead to marginalization of humanity, but coordination or control may prevent this.
Causally separated regions may develop differently, but global integration trends reduce this likelihood.
Gradual integration of humans and AI is plausible, but full merger by 2050 is ambitious.
AI dominance with human survival is a plausible outcome if alignment is partial but not hostile.
Balanced power dynamics between humans and AI are likely if neither fully dominates.
Most probable near-term state: humans retain control as AI advances but remains within delegated bounds.
A fixed system preventing change is possible but requires unprecedented global coordination.
Deliberate abandonment of powerful AI is unlikely given competitive pressures and strategic incentives.

Most near-term human extinction pathways also destroy the fragile compute and energy infrastructure AI depends on, and a misaligned system that kills humanity before achieving self-sufficiency would follow it into collapse. War or bio-catastrophe during the transition window covers the remainder.

This requires human extinction while a value-aligned successor survives on autonomous infrastructure, a narrow conjunction. Most extinction scenarios either take AI down as well or involve systems that do not carry human values.

The largest extinction share is misaligned optimization that removes humans as irrelevant obstacles while continuing under nonhuman goals. It beats The Inheritance because value preservation after human extinction is a narrower target.

If no actor gains a decisive strategic advantage and alignment is only partially solved, multipolar AI competition with sidelined humans is a natural attractor. Diffusion of capability across many labs and states supports this outcome.

Causal separation by 2050 requires self-sustaining off-world settlement or radically isolated enclaves exhibiting different taxonomy states. Even AI-accelerated space industry is unlikely to achieve that within 24 years.

Dominant civilizational merger by 2050 requires mature brain-computer interfaces or whole-brain emulation adopted at scale; augmentation advances but the bar of humans and AI ceasing to be separate agents is high for 24 years of neurotechnology.

Gradual or decisive handover of civilizational steering to AI systems while humans survive without meaningful control covers both paternalistic aligned-AI rule and soft loss of control. Economic and military incentives make delegation past the point of human oversight attractive even absent malice.
